questions.stem: Which is the central bank of India?
questions.explanation: The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) is the central bank of India, established on 1 April 1935 under the RBI Act, 1934, and nationalised in 1949. It regulates the monetary and banking system, issues currency, and acts as the banker to the government and banks. SBI is the largest commercial bank, not the central bank.
questions.subject: Economics

questions.stem: In which year was the Reserve Bank of India established?
questions.explanation: The RBI was established on 1 April 1935 based on the recommendations of the Hilton Young Commission (Royal Commission on Indian Currency and Finance). It was nationalised on 1 January 1949. 1969 was the year of the first major bank nationalisation (14 banks).
questions.subject: Economics

questions.stem: The rate at which the RBI lends money to commercial banks for the short term is called the:
questions.explanation: The Repo Rate (Repurchase Rate) is the rate at which the RBI lends short-term money to commercial banks against government securities. The Reverse Repo Rate is the rate at which RBI borrows from banks. The Repo Rate is a key tool of monetary policy — raising it makes borrowing costlier to curb inflation.
questions.subject: Economics

questions.stem: What does 'CRR' stand for in banking?
questions.explanation: CRR stands for Cash Reserve Ratio — the percentage of a bank's total deposits that it must keep as reserves with the RBI in cash. It is a monetary-policy tool: raising CRR reduces the funds banks can lend (tightening money supply). Unlike SLR, no interest is earned on CRR balances.
questions.subject: Economics

questions.stem: Which bank is the largest public sector commercial bank in India?
questions.explanation: The State Bank of India (SBI) is the largest public sector (and overall) commercial bank in India by assets, deposits, branches, and customers. It traces its origins to the Bank of Calcutta (1806) → Imperial Bank of India → SBI (1955). PNB, Bank of Baroda, and Canara Bank are other large public sector banks.
questions.subject: Economics

questions.stem: How many commercial banks were nationalised in the first round of bank nationalisation in 1969?
questions.explanation: 14 major commercial banks (each with deposits over ₹50 crore) were nationalised on 19 July 1969 under PM Indira Gandhi. A second round in 1980 nationalised 6 more banks. The aim was to extend banking to rural areas and align credit with national priorities like agriculture.
questions.subject: Economics

questions.stem: What does 'SLR' stand for, a regulatory reserve requirement for banks?
questions.explanation: SLR stands for Statutory Liquidity Ratio — the minimum percentage of a bank's net demand and time liabilities (NDTL) that it must maintain in the form of liquid assets such as cash, gold, or approved government securities, before offering credit. Unlike CRR (held in cash with RBI), SLR is held by the bank itself and can earn returns.
questions.subject: Economics

questions.stem: Which body decides the monetary policy (including the repo rate) in India?
questions.explanation: The Monetary Policy Committee (MPC), constituted under the RBI Act (amended 2016), decides the policy repo rate to achieve the inflation target. It has 6 members — 3 from the RBI (including the Governor as chairperson) and 3 appointed by the central government. The inflation target is 4% (±2%). SEBI regulates securities markets, not monetary policy.
questions.subject: Economics

questions.stem: What does 'NPA' stand for in banking?
questions.explanation: NPA stands for Non-Performing Asset — a loan or advance on which the principal or interest payment has remained overdue for 90 days or more. High NPAs weaken a bank's profitability and capital. Mechanisms to deal with NPAs include the SARFAESI Act and the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code (IBC), 2016.
questions.subject: Economics

questions.stem: Which institution is the apex bank for agriculture and rural development in India?
questions.explanation: NABARD (National Bank for Agriculture and Rural Development), established in 1982, is the apex development bank for agriculture and rural development, refinancing rural credit and supporting cooperative and regional rural banks. SIDBI serves small industries; EXIM Bank handles export-import finance; RBI is the central bank.
questions.subject: Economics

questions.stem: What does 'IFSC' code on a cheque/bank account identify?

options.text: A specific bank branch for electronic fund transfers
The interest rate on the account

questions.explanation: IFSC (Indian Financial System Code) is an 11-character alphanumeric code that uniquely identifies a specific bank branch participating in electronic fund transfer systems like NEFT, RTGS, and IMPS. The first 4 characters denote the bank, the 5th is 0, and the last 6 identify the branch.
questions.subject: Economics

questions.stem: Which payment system is used for high-value, real-time fund transfers in India?
questions.explanation: RTGS (Real-Time Gross Settlement) is used for high-value transactions (minimum ₹2 lakh) settled in real time, transaction by transaction. NEFT (National Electronic Funds Transfer) settles in batches and has no minimum limit. Both are now available 24×7. IMPS and UPI provide instant retail transfers.
questions.subject: Economics

questions.stem: UPI (Unified Payments Interface) was developed by which organisation?
questions.explanation: UPI was developed by the National Payments Corporation of India (NPCI), launched in 2016. NPCI is an umbrella organisation for retail payments, set up by the RBI and the Indian Banks' Association. UPI enables instant inter-bank transfers via mobile and has made India a global leader in real-time digital payments. NPCI also runs RuPay and IMPS.
questions.subject: Economics

questions.stem: The currency notes in India (except the ₹1 note) are issued by:
questions.explanation: All currency notes in India except the ₹1 note are issued by the RBI under the RBI Act (signed by the Governor). The ₹1 note and all coins are issued by the Government of India (Ministry of Finance, signed by the Finance Secretary), though distributed through the RBI. This is a classic exam distinction.
questions.subject: Economics

questions.stem: Under the Pradhan Mantri Jan Dhan Yojana (PMJDY), the primary objective was to:

options.text: Achieve financial inclusion by providing bank accounts to every household

questions.explanation: PMJDY, launched in August 2014, aimed at financial inclusion — providing every unbanked household with a basic 'zero-balance' bank account, along with a RuPay debit card, accident insurance, and overdraft facility. It dramatically expanded banking access and underpins Direct Benefit Transfer (DBT) of subsidies.
questions.subject: Economics

questions.stem: What is a 'Small Finance Bank' primarily intended to serve?

options.text: Unserved and underserved sections like small businesses, marginal farmers, and micro industries

questions.explanation: Small Finance Banks (a differentiated bank category licensed by the RBI) primarily serve unserved and underserved sections — small business units, small and marginal farmers, micro and small industries, and the unorganised sector — to further financial inclusion. They must extend a large share of loans to priority sectors. Examples include AU and Equitas Small Finance Banks.
questions.subject: Economics

questions.stem: The deposit insurance in India (covering bank deposits up to ₹5 lakh) is provided by:

options.text: DICGC (Deposit Insurance and Credit Guarantee Corporation)

questions.explanation: Deposit insurance is provided by the DICGC (Deposit Insurance and Credit Guarantee Corporation), a wholly-owned subsidiary of the RBI. Since 2020, it insures bank deposits up to ₹5 lakh per depositor per bank (raised from ₹1 lakh). This protects depositors if a bank fails. IRDAI regulates insurance; SEBI regulates securities markets.
questions.subject: Economics

questions.stem: Which of the following is a function of the RBI as the 'banker's bank'?

options.text: Acting as lender of last resort to commercial banks

questions.explanation: As the 'banker's bank' and lender of last resort, the RBI provides emergency funds to commercial banks facing liquidity crises, holds their reserves (CRR), and acts as a clearing house. The RBI does not deal directly with the public for savings accounts or credit cards — that is the role of commercial banks.
questions.subject: Economics

questions.stem: The first bank to be established in India (one of the earliest) was:
questions.explanation: The Bank of Hindustan (established 1770 in Calcutta) is generally regarded as the first bank in India (now defunct). Among surviving institutions, the lineage of the Bank of Calcutta (1806) led to the Imperial Bank and then SBI. The Allahabad Bank (1865) was the oldest joint-stock bank still operating until its merger in 2020.
questions.subject: Economics

questions.stem: What does 'KYC' stand for, a mandatory process for opening a bank account?
questions.explanation: KYC stands for Know Your Customer — the mandatory process by which banks verify the identity and address of their customers (using documents like Aadhaar, PAN, passport) to prevent money laundering, fraud, and terror financing. RBI guidelines make periodic KYC updation compulsory.
questions.subject: Economics

questions.stem: If the RBI wants to control rising inflation, which monetary-policy action is most appropriate?

options.text: Decrease the repo rate and CRR to inject money
Increase the repo rate and CRR to reduce money supply and curb demand

questions.explanation: To control inflation, the RBI follows a contractionary (tight) monetary policy: it RAISES the repo rate (making borrowing costlier) and may raise the CRR/SLR (reducing banks' lendable funds). This reduces money supply and aggregate demand, easing price pressures. Cutting rates (option A) or printing money would worsen inflation. This is a frequently-tested cause-and-effect.
questions.subject: Economics

questions.stem: What is the key difference between the Repo Rate and the Bank Rate?

options.text: Repo Rate involves lending against collateral (securities) with a repurchase agreement and is short-term; Bank Rate is lending without collateral and is typically longer-term
They are identical with no difference
Bank Rate is set by commercial banks, Repo Rate by the government
Repo Rate applies only to foreign banks

questions.explanation: The Repo Rate is the rate at which the RBI lends to banks SHORT-TERM against collateral (government securities) under a repurchase agreement. The Bank Rate is the rate at which the RBI lends to banks WITHOUT collateral, typically for longer periods, and has no repurchase agreement. The Bank Rate is also linked to the Marginal Standing Facility (MSF). This distinction is a common banking-exam point.
questions.subject: Economics

questions.stem: The Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code (IBC) was enacted in which year to provide a time-bound resolution of bad loans?
questions.explanation: The Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code (IBC) was enacted in 2016 to consolidate and provide a time-bound (originally 180+90 days) framework for resolving insolvency of companies and individuals, helping banks recover bad loans (NPAs). The National Company Law Tribunal (NCLT) adjudicates corporate insolvency cases, and the IBBI regulates the process.
questions.subject: Economics

questions.stem: Which committee's recommendations led to the major banking-sector reforms of the 1990s (including prudential norms and reduction of SLR)?
questions.explanation: The Narasimham Committee (Committee on the Financial System, 1991, and Banking Sector Reforms, 1998) drove the major banking reforms — introducing prudential norms (capital adequacy, income recognition, NPA classification), reducing SLR and CRR, and allowing private/foreign bank entry. The Kelkar and Chelliah committees dealt mainly with tax reforms; Rangarajan with various economic/statistical issues.
questions.subject: Economics

questions.stem: What is 'priority sector lending' (PSL) in Indian banking?

options.text: Lending only to large industrial houses on priority
Giving priority to foreign loan applicants
A mandated minimum share of bank credit directed to sectors like agriculture, MSMEs, education, housing, and weaker sections
Lending only to the central government

questions.explanation: Priority Sector Lending (PSL) is an RBI mandate requiring banks to direct a minimum percentage (currently 40% of Adjusted Net Bank Credit for domestic banks) towards sectors deemed important for inclusive growth — agriculture, micro/small/medium enterprises (MSMEs), education, housing, export credit, and weaker sections. It ensures credit reaches segments that might otherwise be neglected.
questions.subject: Economics
